title: Precious Endgame
reviewNotes: Three branches begin after Qxc6 at 76s, with seven pieces. dxc6 creates the promoted c-pawn, b-pawn races in reply, and Qc5/Qb5/Qc7/Kb4/Qc3 is an actual dovetail mate. Independent Qb6 interposition also ends in actual Qxb6 mate. Independent c8=N loses. The earlier ten-piece setup and eight-piece knight sacrifice remain source context.
transcript: White's brilliant idea is knight to c6 check, forcing the king to b5 because although black is up an entire queen, his king is kind of stuck between the white king and these black pawns. And so after knight to d4 check, the king [music] has to go to a5 and white can play rook to c6, which almost checkmates the black king. If it wasn't for the fact that of course the black knight can go to b5 and cover the checkmate. But I am sure that all of you noticed that both the knight and the rook are attacking that square, which means that white [music] can take the knight and force black to take back with the queen, which means that we can win this queen. So we should, right? Well, not exactly. It is pretty simple to see that after king takes b5, now the black king is able to stop the white pawn from promoting and the white king is way too far to stop the black pawns, which means that black would actually be able to get a queen and win the game. So surprisingly, we have to refrain from winning the queen and find a different way to continue. Well, you might notice that the black king is almost smothered by the white king and the black pieces. So this allows the precise knight to c6 check. And since the black king has no squares, this forces the queen to give itself up. But this time it's of course better for white. We can take back with the pawn and now we have gained a precious tempo towards promotion. But wait a second because black can also get a queen pretty much at the same time. And with both players having still a pawn, this is likely to fizzle out to a draw. But it is white to move and white can play queen to c5 check, forcing queen to b5. And now this position will be a great reminder of the fact that chess is a concrete game because after queen to c7 check, the black king has only one move that doesn't lose the queen right away and that is king b4. But now the black pieces betray their own king because by taking away these two important squares, they allow the surprising queen to c3 with a dovetail checkmate.
